source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199

coverage.scope: C. Exclusions: §§541(b),(c),(d); Patterson v. Shumate; qualified retirement and education assets; postpetition wages; all Problem 3.1(a)-(d)
coverage.notice: IRA and education-account dollar caps quoted in the casebook are indexed and NOT current 2026 figures.

topics.title: C. Exclusions — §541(b), §541(c), §541(d) and Exemption vs Exclusion
topics.description: Basic difference between no estate interest, restricted transfer, trust beneficial rights and later exemption.

entries.title: Exclusion versus §522 exemption: sequence matters
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Statutory exclusions under §541 mean qualifying interest never becomes property of estate. Exempt property enters estate initially but individual debtor claims §522 protection; once allowed, exempt property withdrawn for debtor.
entries.laymanExplanation: Exclusion: basket never takes the item. Exemption: item enters basket then debtor legally removes it.
entries.legalExplanation: Exemptions are for individuals and can be challenged; estate title/inclusion analysis remains necessary before §522.
entries.examApplication: Answer in order: §541(a) included? §541(b)/(c)(2)/(d) limited? If included, §522 exemption?
entries.examTrap: Do not say exempt property never belonged to estate.

entries.title: §541(b): specific excluded categories
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Congress identifies interests outside estate, including certain funds withheld from workers for specified retirement/benefit plans and qualified education funds subject conditions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some money is legally ring-fenced before the trustee ever gets it.
entries.legalExplanation: §541(b)(5),(6),(7) casebook describes special limitations and time windows; read requirements separately.
entries.examApplication: When question gives employee withholding or tuition account, identify precise subsection and beneficiary/date.
entries.examTrap: No universal exemption for all money in retirement or tuition account under §541(b).

entries.title: §541(c)(1): many anti-transfer limitations do not prevent estate entry
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Interests generally enter estate despite certain contractual or legal restrictions on transfers or conditions activated by debtor bankruptcy; exceptions matter.
entries.laymanExplanation: A contract can't usually keep otherwise owned asset out of estate just by saying 'can't sell it on bankruptcy.'
entries.legalExplanation: §541(c)(1) overcomes ordinary anti-alienation/forfeiture effects; §541(c)(2) expressly preserves enforceable restrictions on beneficial interests in trusts.
entries.examApplication: Analyze whether real beneficial trust restraint fits §541(c)(2) instead of generic no-assignment term.
entries.examTrap: Anti-transfer contract term alone isn't equivalent to ERISA-qualified spendthrift trust.

entries.title: §541(d): trustee gets legal title only if debtor held no equitable interest
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Where debtor holds mere legal title and another person holds equitable ownership, estate takes debtor's legal-title interest but not another's equitable interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: If borrower is holding someone else's property in trust, bankruptcy cannot turn it into debtor's beneficial wealth.
entries.legalExplanation: Reflects 'estate takes no more than debtor had' rule; trust rights often governed by nonbankruptcy law.
entries.examApplication: For escrow/trust/hypothetical, identify equitable owner and any trustee duties.
entries.examTrap: The estate never gets more beneficial interest than debtor owned.

entries.title: §541(a)(6): individual Chapter 7 postpetition personal-service income excluded
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Proceeds, rent and profits of estate property generally included, but earnings from services personally performed by an individual debtor after commencement excluded under §541(a)(6).
entries.laymanExplanation: Your new Chapter 7 wages from working after filing are usually yours to keep.
entries.legalExplanation: Purpose of carveout is fresh start; distinguish business goodwill sale proceeds and passive income from actual personal labor.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether payment was earned by individual after filing and whether payment is actually for services.
entries.examTrap: A company cannot use the individual-wages carveout, and §1115/1306 change rule in individual reorganization cases.

entries.title: Sale proceeds versus postpetition wages under §541(a)(6)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: A contract paying in installments after petition may be entirely prepetition capital/asset sale value rather than postpetition services; origin and economic substance control.
entries.laymanExplanation: Getting money in next month's checking account doesn't make it next month's paycheck.
entries.legalExplanation: Andrews provides test when prepetition sale agreement includes noncompetition payments; Segal roots are relevant but not sole wording.
entries.examApplication: Trace contract creation, consideration, date services performed, and timing of payment.
entries.examTrap: Not all conduct that benefits payor qualifies as 'services performed'.

topics.title: C. Patterson v. Shumate — ERISA Anti-Alienation Exclusion
topics.description: Supreme Court full opinion: §541(c)(2) federal nonbankruptcy law, enforceability and plan assets.

entries.title: Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753 (1992)
entries.page: Ch. 3 § C / Patterson opinion (general syllabus pp.171–199)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Yes. 'Applicable nonbankruptcy law' includes federal ERISA as well as state trust law; ERISA-qualified plan's enforceable no-alienation term satisfies §541(c)(2). Supreme Court affirmed, protecting Shumate's vested pension from bankruptcy estate.
entries.laymanExplanation: A debtor's beneficial interest in a trust subject to a restriction on transfer enforceable under applicable nonbankruptcy law—including ERISA—is excluded under §541(c)(2), where statutory elements met.
entries.legalExplanation: Justice Blackmun relied on unqualified statutory text; Congress used 'state law' expressly elsewhere when intended. ERISA §206(d)(1), IRC §401(a)(13) require prohibition on assignment, enforceable via fiduciary duties and civil actions. Creditors couldn't reach pension outside bankruptcy; Butner anti-windfall, retirement security and national consistency support same outcome. Legislative history didn't overcome plain text.
entries.examApplication: Identify ERISA-qualified trust, precise anti-alienation, enforcement mechanism and whether interest is beneficial in trust; compare estate inclusion vs §522 exemptions.
entries.examTrap: Not a blanket exclusion of every retirement account or every personal contractual promise not to assign.
entries.sourceRole: Full Supreme Court opinion excerpt from Chapter 3
entries.facts: Shumate, long-term Coleman Furniture executive, had $250,000 vested interest in ERISA-qualified Coleman pension with express anti-alienation clause. Coleman and Shumate both filed bankruptcy; after plan liquidation trustee Patterson demanded Shumate's share for bankruptcy estate. District court read §541(c)(2) nonbankruptcy law as limited to state spendthrift trusts and ruled plan funds estate property; Fourth Circuit reversed.
entries.issue: Does §541(c)(2)'s exclusion for enforceable restrictions on transfer under 'applicable nonbankruptcy law' include ERISA-required federal pension anti-alienation provisions, allowing qualified pension to stay outside estate?
entries.holding: Yes. 'Applicable nonbankruptcy law' includes federal ERISA as well as state trust law; ERISA-qualified plan's enforceable no-alienation term satisfies §541(c)(2). Supreme Court affirmed, protecting Shumate's vested pension from bankruptcy estate.
entries.reasoning: Justice Blackmun relied on unqualified statutory text; Congress used 'state law' expressly elsewhere when intended. ERISA §206(d)(1), IRC §401(a)(13) require prohibition on assignment, enforceable via fiduciary duties and civil actions. Creditors couldn't reach pension outside bankruptcy; Butner anti-windfall, retirement security and national consistency support same outcome. Legislative history didn't overcome plain text.
entries.rule: A debtor's beneficial interest in a trust subject to a restriction on transfer enforceable under applicable nonbankruptcy law—including ERISA—is excluded under §541(c)(2), where statutory elements met.

entries.title: Why federal ERISA counts as nonbankruptcy law
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Text says 'applicable nonbankruptcy law,' not 'state law,' and can encompass federal statutes governing pensions.
entries.laymanExplanation: A federal pension law is still outside bankruptcy law, so it can protect plan under bankruptcy provision.
entries.legalExplanation: IRS §401(a)(13) and ERISA §206(d)(1) coordinate anti-alienation; enforceability exists through ERISA plan and suits.
entries.examApplication: Look for 'applicable nonbankruptcy law' wording and resist automatically limiting to state spendthrift rules.
entries.examTrap: The nonbankruptcy law must actually make restraint enforceable, not merely express sentiment.

entries.title: ERISA plan fiduciaries and enforceable prohibition
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Plan required benefits neither assigned nor alienated, and ERISA empowered suits to enjoin conduct violating plan's terms; satisfied §541(c)(2) 'enforceable' requirement.
entries.laymanExplanation: It isn't just a private promise; federal law provides teeth.
entries.legalExplanation: §1104(a)(1)(D) fiduciary compliance and §1132 enforcement support.
entries.examApplication: When analyzing a savings account called 'pension,' verify qualified trust and legal restrictions.
entries.examTrap: Unsecured personal retirement savings plan isn't automatically ERISA-trust excluded.

entries.title: Patterson bankruptcy policy: no forum-based pension windfall
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Creditors should not get pension indirectly in bankruptcy if unable to garnish it outside; ERISA protects retirement stream for worker/dependents.
entries.laymanExplanation: Filing should not suddenly make protected nest egg attachable.
entries.legalExplanation: Court ties Butner uniform treatment to ERISA purpose and clear statutory text.
entries.examApplication: In rule synthesis cite §541(c)(2) before §522 retirement exemptions when applicable.
entries.examTrap: Don't treat federal bankruptcy pro-creditor estate scope as superseding clear anti-alienation exception.

entries.title: Who receives Shumate's $250,000?
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Because pension interest was outside estate, Shumate retained claim to payout protected by qualified plan rather than estate trustee using it to pay creditors.
entries.laymanExplanation: Trustee cannot take that pension share for general unsecured creditors.
entries.legalExplanation: Patterson holds exclusion, unlike exemption process which removes estate property later.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish beneficiary of plan, trustee of debtor estate and trustee of pension.
entries.examTrap: Don't say an excluded asset is estate property but later exempted.

topics.title: C. Retirement and Education Account Protections — §541(b) and §522
topics.description: 2005 BAPCPA provisions, inherited IRA, state/federal law retirement protections and indexed 2021 thresholds.

entries.title: §541(b)(7) employee benefit plan payroll withholding
entries.page: Ch. 3 § C / Patterson questions (general syllabus pp.171–199)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: BAPCPA exclusion for specified wages withheld by employer to contribute to ERISA/§403(b)/§457 eligible retirement or health plans, per casebook description.
entries.laymanExplanation: Money properly withheld from paycheck into authorized benefit plan may never become estate property.
entries.legalExplanation: Book notes this exclusion only partially moots Patterson, since employer contributions and later income are not covered in same way.
entries.examApplication: Identify who contributed: employee payroll deduction vs employer money vs investment appreciation.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat all employer-funded pension contributions as §541(b)(7) excluded simply because employee withholding protected.

entries.title: §522(b)(3)(C), §522(d)(12) retirement-fund exemptions
entries.page: Ch. 3 § C / Patterson questions (general syllabus pp.171–199)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: 2005 added bankruptcy exemptions for qualifying tax-exempt retirement funds under IRC §§401,403,408,408A,414,457,501(a), including qualifying traditional/Roth IRAs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some funds may be estate assets but can still be shielded from creditor distribution through exemption.
entries.legalExplanation: This is an EXEMPTION rather than Patterson's EXCLUSION; qualified retirement fund status and applicable caps/rollover rules matter.
entries.examApplication: If ERISA exclusion unavailable, test §522 retirement exemption next.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume exempting every account requires no bankruptcy filing or estate entry.

entries.title: IRA cap as printed in 2021 textbook; indexed
entries.page: Ch. 3 § C / Patterson questions (general syllabus pp.171–199)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Casebook listed IRA-related retirement exemption cap $1,362,800 per debtor / $2,725,600 joint for its edition; these figures may be updated by statutory indexing, not reliable for 2026 calculation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Book's dollar cap is a dated example, not today's legal allowance.
entries.legalExplanation: §522(n) special cap context; distinguish account type, rollover and ordinary IRA issues.
entries.examApplication: If professor's hypothetical uses printed figures, show that they're from assigned book, otherwise verify current indexed amount.
entries.examTrap: Not all retirement fund exemptions subject to same dollar cap.

entries.title: Clark v Rameker inherited IRA treated differently
entries.page: Ch. 3 § C / Patterson questions (general syllabus pp.171–199)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Clark v. Rameker, 573 U.S. 122 (2014), held inherited IRA funds do not qualify as 'retirement funds' under §522 exemptions; inheritor can withdraw for any purpose and isn't saving own retirement.
entries.laymanExplanation: Inherited IRA isn't the same as your own workplace retirement account.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook cites as discussion only (not excerpted majority opinion); characterization turns on statutory purpose and inherited-account rights.
entries.examApplication: Ask original accountholder vs inherited holder and type of IRA.
entries.examTrap: Do not claim every inherited IRA is automatically protected as retirement funds.

entries.title: Rousey v Jacoway IRA support exemption and 2005 expansion
entries.page: Ch. 3 § C / Patterson questions (general syllabus pp.171–199)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Rousey, 544 U.S.320 (2005), held individual retirement accounts may qualify under §522(d)(10)(E) payments reasonably necessary for debtor/dependents; Congress later provided separate broader retirement exemption sections.
entries.laymanExplanation: Old rule protected enough retirement income to live; later Code includes extra retirement-fund routes.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook references Rousey but does not excerpt opinion.
entries.examApplication: Spot the different exemption's 'reasonably necessary' requirement vs later tax-qualified status.
entries.examTrap: Do not mix pre-2005 Rousey limitation into all newer retirement exemptions.

entries.title: §541(b)(5),(6) child/grandchild tuition account exclusions
entries.page: Ch. 3 § C / Patterson questions (general syllabus pp.171–199)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Textbook discusses qualified education IRA and §529 plan funds contributed for child/grandchild at least 365 days before petition; contributions between 365 and 720 days have source-era $6,825 per-beneficiary cap.
entries.laymanExplanation: Depositing for child's college just before filing may not be sheltered, but older qualifying contributions may be excluded.
entries.legalExplanation: Special §541(b)(5),(6) conditions depend on account beneficiary, age of contributions and indexed cap; as of 2021 printed $6,825 figure historical.
entries.examApplication: Construct timeline of deposits 720+ days, 365–720, within 365 and identify qualifying beneficiary.
entries.examTrap: Don't assume anyone's education savings, or recent contributions, entirely excluded.

topics.title: C. Chapter 7 vs 11 vs 13 — Postpetition Earnings and Estate Acquisitions
topics.description: Corporate Chapter 11 new assets, individual Chapter 7 wages, individual Chapter 13 plan earnings, individual Chapter 11 §§1115.

entries.title: Corporate Chapter 11: estate new business earnings generally captured
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: A corporate debtor-in-possession's business operation acquires new estate property and proceeds under §541(a)(6),(7); §1107 debtor in possession generally has trustee authority and §1108 may operate business.
entries.laymanExplanation: Company's sales and new inventory after Chapter 11 filing aren't corporate officers' personal earnings.
entries.legalExplanation: Corporations are not individual debtors eligible for §541(a)(6) personal services exclusion.
entries.examApplication: For Debtor Inc. compare prepetition equipment and postpetition receivables/inventory.
entries.examTrap: Don't take officer's individual wage exception and apply it to the corporate debtor.

entries.title: Worker A Chapter 7: postpetition service wages excluded
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Natural person Chapter 7's postfiling salary from actual labor ordinarily stays outside estate under §541(a)(6), while petition-date bank accounts and accrued wage rights can enter.
entries.laymanExplanation: Worker A generally keeps wages earned from work performed after filing.
entries.legalExplanation: Need distinguish paycheck paid afterward but earned before filing; the labor service date can matter.
entries.examApplication: In hypothetical ask which pay period wages correspond to.
entries.examTrap: Don't classify all checks received after filing as postpetition earnings.

entries.title: Worker B Chapter 13: §1306 broadens estate to postpetition earnings
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: §1306 generally adds postpetition property and personal-service earnings through case milestones for Chapter 13, coordinating plan funding and §1322/§1325; vesting under §1327 can affect property status.
entries.laymanExplanation: Worker B must generally use later earnings to finance a 3–5 year repayment plan, unlike Worker A Chapter 7.
entries.legalExplanation: Chapter 13's express provision supplements baseline §541(a)(6) worker protection; interpret plan confirmation/vesting provision where relevant.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish property-of-estate legal status and disposable income required in plan.
entries.examTrap: Do not claim §541(a)(6) wage exclusion defeats §1306.

entries.title: Prez individual Chapter 11: §1115 expands estate
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: For natural-person Chapter 11, §1115 generally includes postpetition property acquisitions and earnings from debtor's services while case active, enabling reorganization plan payments.
entries.laymanExplanation: CEO filing personal Chapter 11 may have future pay included for restructuring even if own employer also has a Chapter 11.
entries.legalExplanation: §1115 and §§1123(a)(8),1129(a)(15) link future income to individual plans; §1141 discharge/vesting effects distinct.
entries.examApplication: Analyze CEO individual estate separately from corporation's separate estate; do not merge assets.
entries.examTrap: The corporation and its CEO are different debtors and separate §541 estates.

entries.title: §541(a)(6) earnings versus §541(a)(7) estate acquisitions
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
entries.summary: Company's postpetition business property acquired by estate enters under §541(a)(7); individual's new labor can be excluded under §541(a)(6), except reorganization chapters overriding by §§1306/1115.
entries.laymanExplanation: Ask who earned/acquired and which chapter, not just date of check.
entries.legalExplanation: Create 4-case table: corporation Ch11, individual Ch7, individual Ch13, individual Ch11.
entries.examApplication: For each wages/property issue: prepetition interest? postpetition earnings? special chapter?
entries.examTrap: Don't conflate estate assets of separately filing people or operating company.

problems.title: Problem 3.1
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), uploaded Chapter 3 § C, Patterson v Shumate, Problem 3.1; Effross Fall 2026 syllabus general pp.171–199
problems.prompt: Problem 3.1 four linked hypothetical debtors on May 1: (a) Debtor Inc., operating Chapter 11 as DIP and generating postpetition business property, identify estate property §§541(a)(1),(6),(7),1107,1108; (b) its employee Worker A filed Chapter 7 and earned new wages; (c) employee Worker B filed Chapter 13 and earned new wages, use §§1306,1322,1325,1327,1328; (d) CEO Prez separately filed individual Chapter 11 and continued earning pay, use §§1115,1123,1129,1141. Compare inclusion of new property and wages under each chapter; leave all four subparts unanswered.
